hints: Compare the words in option A with the definition of force from momentum: does it mention per unit time or rate?
Check units: force is in $\text{N}$ which is $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$, while change of momentum is in $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ - what is missing?
Test the other word equations by rearranging $F = ma$, $moment = Fd$ and $W = Fs$ to see if they give force correctly.
walkthrough: List what each word equation claims: B is $F = ma$, C is $F = moment/distance$, D is $F = work/displacement$, and A is $F = change$ $of$ $momentum$.
Recall the momentum form of Newton's second law: $F = rate$ $of$ $change$ $of$ $momentum = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Check units to confirm: $\Delta p$ has units $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ but $F$ has units $\text{N} = \text{kg m s}^{-2}$, so division by time $\text{s}$ is needed.

Verify B, C and D are correct rearrangements of $F=ma$, $moment = force \times perpendicular$ $distance$ $from$ $the$ $pivot$, and $work$ $done = force \times displacement$ $in$ $the$ $direction$ $of$ $the$ $force$.
Therefore only the statement that force equals change of momentum without rate is not correct. This is option A

options.A: Force equals rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, not just $\Delta p$. The word equation misses division by time.
options.B: This is Newton's second law, $F = ma$, which is correct for constant mass.
options.C: Since $moment = force \times perpendicular distance$, rearrangement to $force = moment / distance$ is correct.
options.D: Since $work done = force \times displacement$, rearrangement to $force = work done / displacement$ is correct.
